_note: Hand-authored repairs applied by lint-grammar-bank.mjs --fix. Patch only where the fix is unambiguous (a real Polish-learner error as the third option, a recycled distractor replaced by a parallel one, a mis-filed concept moved home). Everything else is deleted. Items may carry an optional 'prompt' when 'Which sentence is correct?' would be ambiguous because the distractor is grammatical but means something else.

options: I have a dog and a cat.
I have dog and a cat.
I went to an store yesterday.
I went to the store yesterday.
articles_5.explain: A place both speakers know takes 'the': the store, the station. Polish has no article to drop, so the bare noun feels complete but is not.

options: I want to become a doctor.
I want to become an doctor.
articles_8.explain: Jobs take a/an even after 'become': become a doctor. Polish 'zostać lekarzem' has no article, so learners drop it.

options: She is teacher at my school.
She is a teacher at my school.
She is an teacher at my school.
articles_9.explain: Jobs take a/an: a teacher, an engineer. Polish has no articles, so 'teacher' alone feels complete but is not.

articles_13.explain: Singular countable nouns need an article, and 'an' before a vowel sound: an office. Polish has no articles, so learners omit them.

options: At the weekend, I go to the cinema.
In weekend I go to cinema.
At the weekend, I go to cinema.
articles_14.explain: 'The cinema' takes 'the' even in general (like 'the theatre', 'the gym'). Polish 'w weekend' has no article, so both get dropped.

options: She is a very nice person.
She is an very nice person.
articles_18.explain: a + adjective + noun: a very nice person. Polish has no articles, so the whole phrase feels complete without one.

options: I am a student from Poland.
I am an student from Poland.
When I am older, I will have a house.
When I am older, I will have house.
When I am older, I will have an house.
articles_29.explain: A new, singular countable thing takes 'a': a house. Polish has no article to drop, so the bare noun feels finished but is not.

articles_33.explain: Singular countable nouns need an article, and 'an' before a vowel sound: an accurate translation.

articles_34.explain: English needs both the verb 'is' and the article: Today is a rainy day. Polish 'Dziś deszczowy dzień' has neither.

options: He is in hospital with a broken leg.
He is in a hospital with a broken leg.
He is in hospitals with a broken leg.
articles_1.explain: British English: in hospital (as a patient), in prison, at school, no article. Americans say 'in the hospital'.

verb_tense_0.explain: Routine = present simple: I work. Polish 'Pracuję' is one word, so learners either drop 'am' from a continuous form or add it to a simple one.

options: I didn't wake up early today.
I didn't woke up early today.
I don't wake up early today.
verb_tense_4.explain: A finished action earlier today takes past simple: didn't + base verb (wake, not woke). Polish uses the present for 'today' events.

options: I have had a party yesterday.
verb_tense_7.explain: 'Yesterday' is finished time, so past simple: had. Never present perfect with yesterday.

verb_tense_10.explain: Present perfect continuous with she/he/it: has been + -ing.

verb_tense_17.explain: After didn't the verb goes back to its base form: didn't go. Polish marks the past on the verb itself (nie poszedłem), so learners mark it twice.

verb_tense_18.explain: Only he/she/it takes 'has'; they have. Polish 'oni mają' looks the same for every plural subject, so the -s rule is easy to forget.

options: Water is boiling at 100 degrees every time.

verb_tense_26.explain: 'Yesterday' forces past simple, and go is irregular: went.

verb_tense_29.explain: 'People' is plural: people work. A sentence also needs a finite verb, so 'working' alone is not enough.

options: I've waiting for him since morning.
I've been waiting for him since morning.
I'm waiting for him since morning.
verb_tense_35.explain: since + present perfect continuous: have been waiting. Polish uses the present with 'od' (since), which pulls learners to 'I'm waiting'.

verb_tense_38.explain: did = past simple, done = past participle (have done). Simple past on its own: I did it.

options: My brother is have my bike.
verb_tense_40.explain: he/she/it (my brother) takes 'has'. Polish 'mieć' looks the same for every person, so the -s is easy to miss.

options: I have already see that film.
I have already seen that film.
I have already saw that film.
This time next week I will lying on a beach.
This time next week I will be lying on a beach.
This time next week I am lie on a beach.

subject_verb_0.explain: Present continuous needs the auxiliary that matches the subject: I am working. Polish 'pracuję' has no auxiliary, so learners drop it.

subject_verb_16.explain: Third person: doesn't + base verb (no second -s). Polish learners learn 'don't' first and use it for everyone.

options: My family are live in Warsaw.

subject_verb_17.explain: Plural subjects take 'were': they were. Polish 'byli' does not change the auxiliary, so was/were is easy to mix up.

subject_verb_18.explain: Third person singular takes 'has': she has finished.

options: Can you explain me one more time?
Can you explain to me one more time?
Can you explain at me one more time?
prepositions_3.explain: explain something TO someone. Polish 'wyjaśnić mi' needs no preposition, which is why 'explain me' feels right.

prepositions_6.explain: interested IN. Polish 'zainteresowany czymś' uses a case ending, not a preposition, so any English preposition feels equally likely.

prepositions_15.explain: depend ON. Polish 'zależeć od' ('from') is why 'depend from' feels natural.

prepositions_29.explain: afraid OF. Polish 'bać się czegoś' uses a case ending, so learners guess a preposition; 'from' comes from 'od'.

prepositions_33.explain: 'discuss' takes its object directly: discuss something (but talk ABOUT something). Polish 'dyskutować o' has a preposition, English does not.

prepositions_14.explain: agree WITH a person (agree TO a proposal). Polish 'zgadzać się z' matches 'with'.

plurals_17.explain: responsible FOR. Polish 'odpowiedzialny za' maps to 'for'.

word_order_5.explain: Questions need do/does, and after 'does' the verb loses its -s: Where does she live?

word_order_13.explain: Time words go at the end (or the very start), never between subject and verb: I am going tomorrow.

word_order_26.explain: 'also' goes before the main verb: I also want to go. 'too' only works at the end: I want to go too.

options: She always drinks tea in the morning.
She drinks tea always in the morning.
She drinks always tea in the morning.
She gave to me the book.
He has made a good progress.
plurals_4.explain: 'progress' is uncountable, so never 'a progress'. Polish 'ma duży postęp' invites the article and the wrong verb.

options: She gave me a lot of advices.
She gave me a lot of advice.
She gave me a lot of advises.
plurals_13.explain: 'advice' is uncountable: never 'advices'. (Same for information, furniture, news.)

options: I have a lot of work
I have a lot of works
plurals_2.explain: 'work' (a job, tasks) is uncountable: a lot of work, not 'works' and not 'very much work' in an affirmative sentence.

modals_8.explain: will + base verb: will go. No -ing and no 'to' after a modal.

modals_1.prompt: Which sentence tells a friend that coming is optional?
options: You don't must come if you're busy.
You mustn't come if you're busy.
You don't have to come if you're busy.
If you heated ice, it melts.
If you heat ice, it will melted.
If you heat ice, it melts.
She is the most good student in the class.
She is the goodest student in the class.
She is the best student in the class.
He stopped to smoke last year.
In the morning I wake up.
In the morning I wake on.
collocation_10.explain: 'wake up' is a phrasal verb; the particle 'up' is part of the meaning (Polish 'budzić się' is one verb).

questions_negation_5.explain: MAKE an appointment (and plans, decisions, mistakes). Polish 'zrobić' covers both make and do.

options: Let me tell to you something.
word_choice_16.explain: tell + person (tell you), say + words (say something). Polish 'powiedzieć ci coś' is one verb for both.

word_choice_21.prompt: You want to say that at the moment you work from home. Which is right?
word_choice_21.explain: False friend: Polish 'aktualnie' = currently. English 'actually' means 'in fact', so the first sentence says something different.

word_choice_29.prompt: You want to say you are sad about something. Which is right?
options: I feel sorry for about this.
word_choice_29.explain: False friend: Polish 'patetyczny' (solemn, moving) is not English 'pathetic' (pitiful, useless). To express regret say 'I feel sorry about this'.

word_choice_31.prompt: You want to say that at the moment you are very tired. Which is right?
word_choice_31.explain: False friend: Polish 'aktualnie' = currently (at present). English 'actually' = in fact. 'Actually, I'm very tired' is good English but says something else.

word_choice_30.prompt: You want to say your sister's feelings are easily hurt (wrażliwa). Which is right?

questions_negation_1.explain: Questions need do/does: What do you want? Polish asks with intonation alone ('Co chcesz?'), so the auxiliary is easy to leave out.

options: Your opinion is very important for me.
Your opinion is very important to me.
Your opinion is very important at me.
add.explain: When something matters to a person's feelings, English says 'important TO me'. Polish 'ważne dla mnie' pulls learners toward 'for'. ('Important FOR' = good for a purpose: 'Sleep is important for your health.')

options: Sleep is important to your health.
Sleep is important for your health.
Sleep is important with your health.
add.explain: 'Important FOR' = necessary or good for a purpose or benefit: for your health, for the exam. 'Important TO' = it matters to a person.

options: If I will see him, I will tell him.
If I see him, I will tell him.
If I would see him, I will tell him.
add.explain: First conditional: if + present simple, will + verb. Polish puts the future in both halves ('jeśli go zobaczę'); English never puts 'will' after 'if'.

options: If I was you, I would took the job.
If I were you, I would take the job.
If I would be you, I would take the job.
add.explain: Second conditional advice: If I were you, I would take… 'would' never goes inside the if-clause.

options: If you had told me, I would help you.
If you had told me, I would have helped you.
If you would have told me, I would have helped you.
add.explain: Third conditional (a past regret): if + had + participle, would have + participle.

options: This phone is the most cheap in the shop.
This phone is the cheapest in the shop.
This phone is cheapest than the others.
add.explain: One-syllable adjectives take -est for the superlative: the cheapest. Comparing two things uses -er + than: cheaper than.

options: Warsaw is much bigger as Kraków.
Warsaw is much bigger than Kraków.
Warsaw is much more bigger than Kraków.
